cards.title: Eight planets, one star
cards.body: Our solar system has one star (the Sun) and eight planets: Mercury, Venus, Earth, Mars, Jupiter, Saturn, Uranus, Neptune. The four inner ones are small and rocky; the four outer ones are gas and ice giants. Pluto was reclassified as a dwarf planet in 2006.

cards.title: Order matters
cards.body: From the Sun outward: Mercury (scorched), Venus (crushing greenhouse heat), Earth (just right), Mars (cold desert), then the giants — Jupiter (biggest), Saturn (rings), Uranus (tipped sideways), Neptune (windiest). Distance from the Sun sets the thermostat.
Memorize the order with: 'My Very Educated Mother Just Served Us Nachos' — Mercury, Venus, Earth, Mars, Jupiter, Saturn, Uranus, Neptune.

Light from the Sun takes 8 minutes to reach Earth — so you're always seeing the Sun as it was 8 minutes ago. From Neptune, it's over 4 hours. The solar system is so big that 'now' depends on where you stand.

cards.q: Why is Pluto not a planet?
choices: It hasn't cleared its orbit of other objects
It's made of ice, not rock
cards.explain: The 2006 definition demands a planet clear its orbital neighborhood. Pluto shares its zone with Kuiper Belt objects, so it's a dwarf planet.

flashcards.front: How many planets are in our solar system?
flashcards.back: Eight: Mercury, Venus, Earth, Mars, Jupiter, Saturn, Uranus, Neptune.
Jupiter — more massive than all other planets combined.

flashcards.front: Which planet has the famous rings?
flashcards.back: Saturn (though Jupiter, Uranus, and Neptune have faint rings too).

flashcards.front: How long does sunlight take to reach Earth?

questions.q: Put in order from the Sun: Mars, Venus, Mercury
questions.explain: Mercury is closest, then Venus, then Earth, then Mars. The inner rocky lineup never changes.

questions.q: The four outer planets are mostly...?
questions.explain: Jupiter and Saturn are gas giants; Uranus and Neptune are ice giants. The rocky ones are all inner.

questions.q: Venus is hotter than Mercury because...?
choices: A runaway greenhouse effect traps heat
questions.explain: Mercury is closer, but Venus's thick CO₂ atmosphere traps heat so completely it's the hottest planet — about 465°C.

choices: A ring of icy objects beyond Neptune
questions.explain: It's the donut of dwarf planets and comets past Neptune — Pluto's neighborhood, and the reason Pluto got demoted.
Uranus rolls around the Sun tilted 98 degrees — likely from an ancient collision. It has 28 known moons, so it's not lonely.

cards.title: The Sun is just a star
cards.body: Every star you see at night is a sun — some bigger, some smaller than ours. Stars shine because their cores fuse hydrogen into helium, releasing enormous energy. Our Sun is aggressively average: a middle-aged, middle-sized star in a quiet neighborhood.

cards.title: Galaxies are star cities
cards.body: A galaxy is a vast collection of stars, gas, and dust held together by gravity. Ours is the Milky Way — about 100 billion stars in a spiral. The nearest big neighbor, Andromeda, is 2.5 million light-years away and drifting toward us.
A light-year is a distance, not a time: how far light travels in one year — about 9.5 trillion kilometers. When astronomers say a star is 100 light-years away, they mean its light left 100 years ago.
Look at the Andromeda galaxy tonight (it's visible as a faint smudge). The light hitting your eyes left 2.5 million years ago — before humans existed. Stargazing is time travel.

cards.explain: Stars fuse hydrogen into helium, converting mass to energy. It's not burning and not reflected — it's nuclear physics, the same process as a hydrogen bomb, sustained for billions of years.

flashcards.back: A star — a middle-aged, average-sized one.
A huge collection of stars, gas, and dust bound by gravity.
The distance light travels in one year (~9.5 trillion km).

flashcards.front: Which galaxy do we live in?
flashcards.back: The Milky Way — a spiral with ~100 billion stars.

questions.explain: Fusion in the core: hydrogen nuclei merge into helium, and the missing mass becomes light and heat. Fission (splitting) is power plants, not stars.

questions.q: Andromeda is 2.5 million light-years away. Its light...?
questions.explain: Light speed is fast but finite. Every star you see is a message from the past — Andromeda's is just a very old one.
The Milky Way is a barred spiral — a flat disk with arms winding out from the center. We sit about two-thirds of the way out.

questions.q: The Sun is best described as...?
questions.explain: It's a G-type main-sequence star, about 4.6 billion years old with 5 billion to go. Spectacularly ordinary — which is great for us.

questions.q: What happens when a massive star dies?
choices: It can collapse into a black hole
questions.explain: Stars over ~20 solar masses go supernova and their cores can collapse past neutron stars into black holes — gravity winning completely.

cards.title: We walked on the Moon in 1969
cards.body: On July 20, 1969, Apollo 11 landed Neil Armstrong and Buzz Aldrin on the Moon while Michael Collins orbited above. Armstrong's first step was watched by 600 million people. Twelve humans have walked on the Moon — all American, all between 1969 and 1972.

cards.title: Robots go where we can't
cards.body: No human has been to Mars, but rovers like Perseverance are there now, drilling rocks and flying a helicopter. Voyager 1, launched in 1977, is the farthest human-made object — it crossed into interstellar space carrying a golden record of Earth sounds.

Remember the firsts: first satellite (Sputnik, 1957), first human in space (Yuri Gagarin, 1961), first Moon landing (Apollo 11, 1969), first space station crew (ISS, 2000 — continuously occupied since).
The ISS orbits Earth every 90 minutes at 28,000 km/h. Astronauts up there see 16 sunrises a day. It's been continuously occupied since November 2000 — the longest human presence off Earth.

cards.q: How many people have walked on the Moon?
cards.explain: Twelve, all from NASA's Apollo program (1969–1972). Nobody has been back since Apollo 17 — though Artemis aims to change that.

flashcards.front: When did humans first land on the Moon?
Who was the first human in space?
What was the first artificial satellite?
flashcards.back: Sputnik 1, launched by the USSR in 1957.
The International Space Station — continuously occupied since 2000.

questions.explain: Armstrong and Aldrin walked; Collins stayed in the command module orbiting above. Gagarin was Soviet and never went to the Moon.

choices: It's the farthest human-made object from Earth
questions.explain: Launched 1977, it passed the heliopause into interstellar space in 2012. No crew — just instruments and the Golden Record.

questions.q: The ISS has been continuously occupied since...?
questions.explain: Expedition 1 arrived November 2000. Every day since, at least one human has been in orbit — over two decades straight.

questions.q: What does Perseverance do on Mars?
choices: Studies rocks and searches for signs of ancient life
questions.explain: It's a rolling science lab: drilling core samples, testing oxygen production, and flying the Ingenuity helicopter.

questions.q: Why haven't humans been to Mars yet?
questions.explain: It's a 7-month trip each way through radiation, with no resupply and a thin unbreathable atmosphere. Mars does have gravity — about 38% of Earth's.
